program: SNAP — Indiana uses the plain federal program name throughout FSSA/DFR materials and its own Program Policy Manual; Indiana does NOT give the food-assistance program itself a state brand name, though its EBT card carries the brand name "Hoosier Works"
agency: Indiana Family and Social Services Administration (FSSA), Division of Family Resources (DFR)
agency_short: Indiana Family and Social Services Administration (FSSA)
admin_note: Indiana is STATE-administered: FSSA is the state agency responsible for social service and financial assistance programs, and the Division of Family Resources (DFR) — one of FSSA's seven major service divisions — has statewide responsibility for SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid. DFR's county-level "local offices" are the state agency's own field offices (FSSA's own manual describes FSSA as "responsible for ensuring federal regulations are initially implemented and consistently applied in each county"), not independently governed county welfare departments the way Virginia's LDSS or North Carolina's county DSS are — matching the administrative archetype this roster's Georgia and Tennessee packs document, not the county-administered archetype. Confirm current operative practice (processing times, local outreach materials, exact office procedures) with the applicant's own DFR local office, the same caution this roster already carries for CA/NY/MN/WI/OH/NC/NJ/VA.
system: Indiana's eligibility caseworkers use the state's ICES (Indiana Client Eligibility System) case-management system; applicants apply through the FSSA Benefits Portal or in person/by mail/fax at a DFR local office

verification.method: Direct curl fetch (browser User-Agent) of eight current FSSA Division of Family Resources Program Policy Manual chapter PDFs (1000/2000/2200/2400/2600/3000/3200/3400, plus the full integrated ICES_Program_Policy_Manual.pdf) from in.gov/fssa/dfr/files — every fetch returned a clean HTTP 200, converted to text with pdftotext -layout, and searched for categorical eligibility, resource limits, vehicle treatment, utility standards, deductions, ABAWD provisions, expedited service, and certification-period sections. The Indiana General Assembly's own statute-lookup site (iga.in.gov) returned HTTP 200 but is a client-side JavaScript single-page application with no server-rendered statutory text (confirmed by inspecting the raw HTML: a bare <div id="root"> and a bundled JS file, no article text) — a genuine, disclosed tooling barrier, not treated as a successful primary-text fetch. law.justia.com returned HTTP 403 and casetext.com returned HTTP 410 on every attempt (multiple User-Agents, both http and https) for Ind. Code Ann. § 12-14-30-3's full text. The drug-felony finding instead rests on convergent corroboration from Indiana's own FSSA FAQ page (faqs.in.gov, fetched directly), the Public Health Law Center's SNAP Ban Opt-Out States map (Indiana entry, fetched directly), and the Network for Public Health Law's compiled 50-state SNAP felony-ban survey PDF (fetched directly, Indiana row parsed from its table). Also fetched and cross-checked: USDA's official States that Operate a Restaurant Meals Program list (Indiana absent), USDA's FY2025-2029 ABAWD Time Limit Waivers index page, and abawdmap.us (independent aggregator, corroborating zero active Indiana waivers, cross-checked against Indiana's own Program Policy Manual language that there are 'currently no such designations').
verification.gates: Unlike Tennessee's pack in this roster, Indiana's own Program Policy Manual publishes CURRENT, dated, Indiana-specific dollar figures for every dollar-denominated SNAP standard this pack needed: the resource limits ($3,000 standard / $4,500 elderly-or-disabled, effective 10/01/2024), the income standards (130% gross / 100% net FPL, effective 10/01/2025, with the full AG-size chart), the four-tier Standard Utility Allowance ($486 heating/cooling, $283 non-heating/cooling, $62 single utility, $36 telephone, effective 10/01/2025), the Standard Deduction ($209/$209/$209/$223/$261/$299 by household size, effective 10/01/2025), the Excess Shelter Expense Deduction cap ($744, effective 10/01/2025), and the Homeless Shelter Deduction ($198.99, effective 10/1/2025) — all of these dollar figures match the current FFY2026 federal COLA-adjusted figures this roster's other packs (e.g. Virginia's) have already independently confirmed, so no dollar-figure gap exists in this pack unlike Tennessee's. The one genuine access limitation is Indiana's own statute text for the drug-felony provision (Ind. Code Ann. § 12-14-30-3): iga.in.gov's own site is a client-rendered SPA this pack's tooling could not execute, and both third-party statute-text mirrors this pack tried (law.justia.com, casetext.com) failed outright (HTTP 403 and HTTP 410 respectively) — a genuine, disclosed barrier, resolved through convergent corroboration from Indiana's own FAQ page plus two independent legal-research secondary sources, the same resolution path Tennessee's pack in this roster used for its own drug-felony finding.
